lines: Jamie Alvarez
+1 (555) 010-5820 | jamie.alvarez@example.com | example.com/in/jalvarez
EDUCATION
Riverbend Polytechnic | B.S. in Industrial Engineering | Metro City, USA | Sep 2014 - May 2018
EXPERIENCE
Greenleaf Florist | Delivery Driver and Shop Assistant | Metro City, USA | Sep 2025 - Present
- Delivered 30 to 40 arrangements a day across the city and took cash and card payments at the door.
- Prepared weekend wedding orders with the head florist and kept the cooler stocked and labeled.
Lakeview Distribution | Operations Analyst | Metro City, USA | Jul 2018 - Jan 2021
- Raised forecast accuracy from 70% to 85% by switching the MAPE calculation to cover only SKUs that sold every week.
- Ran a time study of the returns desk; my findings led to a triage station that cut returns processing time from 3 days to 1.
- Wrote the dock scheduling rules for 12 carriers, cutting average trailer wait at the dock from 95 to 40 minutes.
- Set up cycle counting for the 2,000 highest-value locations, raising inventory record accuracy from 91% to 98.5% within a year.
Crestway Foods | Supply Chain Planner | Metro City, USA | Feb 2021 - Jul 2025
- Rebuilt weekly demand planning for 1,400 SKUs across 3 distribution centers with a seasonal forecast model, cutting stockouts from 6.2% to 2.8% while inventory fell by $1.9M.
- Cut inbound freight cost per pallet from $48 to $41 over two quarters by consolidating supplier pickups into four regional milk runs.
- Set reorder points for every SKU from 18 months of daily demand and supplier lead-time data, reviewed monthly with the category managers.

- Scoring 40 vendors weekly on on-time delivery, fill rate, lead-time variance and invoice accuracy, and sharing the scorecards with buyers before each quarterly review, raised on-time inbound deliveries from 81% to 93%.
- Raised the packaging line's overall equipment effectiveness (OEE) from 71% to 112% by cutting changeover time and micro-stops.
- Trained 6 planners on the new forecasting workflow and wrote its exception-handling guide, which the team still uses for promotions.
PROJECTS
Last-Mile Routing Study | Independent Project | Python | Oct 2024 - Present
- Modeled a regional grocer's 85 daily delivery stops as a vehicle-routing problem, cutting planned route miles 18% against the grocer's current routes.
- Cut average route length from 120 to 90 miles, a 40% reduction, by solving the routing problem with customer time windows.
- Raised on-time deliveries by 9% in simulation, from 84% to 93%, by adding customer time windows to the routing model.
Regional Food Bank Warehouse | Volunteer Consultant, Team of 4 | Excel | Mar 2022 - Jul 2022
- Analyzed warehouse operations and made recommendations to the food bank's leadership.
- The donation intake process was mapped and two duplicate data-entry steps were removed, so donations reached the shelves a day sooner.
- Wrote a slotting guide that the volunteer coordinators used to re-slot the warehouse again after its spring expansion.
SKILLS
Tools: Excel, Python
Methods: demand forecasting, inventory planning, time studies, vehicle routing

items.says: The experience entries are not in reverse chronological order.
items.because: Lakeview appears above the more recent Crestway role, making the work history harder to scan.

items.says: Education appears before the stronger work history.
items.because: A reader may not see the most relevant professional experience as quickly.

items.says: The current florist entry is longer than needed for the operations and supply-chain direction.
items.because: Its shop and delivery duties do not advance that direction.

items.says: The delivery bullet gives volume and duties but no outcome.
items.because: The reader cannot see what the work achieved.

items.says: The wedding-order bullet does not explain what preparing the orders involved.
items.because: “Prepared” could describe a range of tasks, so the candidate’s contribution is unclear.

items.says: The wedding-order bullet lists responsibilities without showing what they accomplished.
The forecast-accuracy increase is not a valid like-for-like comparison.
items.because: Excluding SKUs that did not sell every week changes the population measured and can make the metric look better without improving forecasts.

items.says: The description of which SKUs the MAPE calculation covers is wordy and imprecise.
The time-study bullet uses a first-person pronoun.
The candidate’s role in putting the triage station in place is indirect.
items.because: “My findings led to” does not say whether the candidate helped implement it.

items.says: The returns-processing comparison does not define the days.
The dock-scheduling bullet does not say what the rules governed.
“At the dock” repeats context already conveyed by “trailer wait.”
The inventory-accuracy figures do not identify the population they measure.
items.because: The improvement could apply to the 2,000 counted locations or to a broader inventory population.

items.says: The demand-planning bullet puts its impact after the scope and method.
items.because: A scanning reader must reach the end to find the stockout and inventory results.

items.says: “A seasonal forecast model” is too general to show the specific forecasting approach.
The reorder-point bullet gives no result.
items.because: A reader cannot tell whether the work improved availability, reduced excess inventory, or otherwise helped the business.

items.says: The monthly-review phrase shifts attention to a recurring duty.
items.because: It makes the bullet sound more like an ongoing responsibility than a completed action.

items.says: The vendor-scorecard bullet opens awkwardly.
items.because: The participial opening makes the causal link between the scorecards and delivery improvement unclear.

items.says: The vendor-scorecard bullet buries its result after lengthy process details.
items.because: A scanning reader may not reach the strongest evidence of the work’s value.

items.says: The OEE figure of 112% is impossible under the conventional OEE definition.
items.because: Availability, performance, and quality are each bounded at 100%, so conventional OEE cannot exceed 100%.

items.says: The OEE bullet names areas of improvement but not the specific intervention.
The guide’s use for promotions does not show what it improved.
The 120-to-90-mile change is a 25% reduction, not 40%.
items.because: The decrease is 30 miles, or 25% of the original 120 miles, and the stated percentage also conflicts with the other route-mile result.

items.says: “Average route length” does not say which routes the average covers.
items.because: The measure is harder to interpret without the comparison population.

items.says: The route-mile result is repeated across two bullets in the same study.
items.because: Both bullets report reducing route miles and may read as duplicate evidence for the same result.

items.says: The time-window intervention is repeated from the preceding bullet.
items.because: Both bullets describe adding customer time windows, so they read as though they report the same intervention.

items.says: The warehouse-analysis bullet gives no scope or approach.
The warehouse-analysis bullet does not say what changed as a result.
“Made recommendations” is broad and does not specify the action taken.
The intake-process bullet uses passive voice, obscuring the candidate’s role.
items.because: A reader cannot tell who mapped the process or removed the duplicate steps.

items.says: The intake-process bullet puts its clearest impact late in the line.
items.because: Donations reaching shelves sooner appears after the background.

items.says: The slotting-guide bullet does not show the expertise it captured.
The slotting-guide bullet does not show the result of the re-slotting.
“Again” is redundant after “re-slot.”
